podcast.title: Ambitions for Fame and Fortune (1975)
podcast.body: In the summer of 1975, Gary Gashhorn articulated the band's desire for mainstream success, including gold albums, European tours, movies, and financial gain, acknowledging it would be "stupid to say we're in it for another reason other than to expand our wallets." "we want it all like gold albums a European tour lots of movies we'd be stupid to say we're in it for another reason other than to expand our wallets."

podcast.title: "Amy" Inspiring Names
podcast.body: Many people reportedly named their daughters after Pure Prairie League's song "Amy." The song is described as embodying elements of country rock: twang, harmonies, and heartache. "A lot of people though seem to have named their daughters after the song"

podcast.title: College Radio's Role in Revival
podcast.body: Despite being dropped by RCA and their album "Bustin' Out" being out of print, college radio stations continued to play tracks from the album, particularly "Amy." This grassroots support eventually caught the attention of country and Top 40 radio, leading to RCA re-signing the band and the song's re-release as a successful single, giving the band "new life." "but it was college radio not mainstream radio that made that happen."

podcast.title: Craig Fuller's Legal Problems
podcast.body: Co-founder Craig Fuller's legal issues stemming from claiming conscientious objector status during the Vietnam War draft significantly impacted the band. In 1973 (the year US troops withdrew), he was sentenced to six months in prison in Springfield, Missouri, followed by two years of service in an "alternative mental hospital." These problems contributed to RCA dropping the band after their "Bustin' Out" album was released. "Now granted Craig Fuller one of the band's co-founders created some issues because he claimed conscientious objector status with the draft board when he refused to report for the draft for the Vietnam war and was sentenced to six months in prison in Springfield, Missouri in 1973."

podcast.title: Craig Fuller's Return and Departure
podcast.body: Craig Fuller eventually rejoined Pure Prairie League but did not stay for long. His preference for a more rock-oriented sound diverged from the band's collective direction, leading to his eventual departure. "Craig Fuller did eventually rejoin the band but he just didn't stay very long and I think that pure prairie league was okay with that he was more into rock than they collectively wanted to be."

podcast.title: Mike Reilly Stepping Up
podcast.body: After Craig Fuller's legal troubles led to RCA dropping Pure Prairie League, Mike Reilly joined the band and "stepped up" to "grab the reins" and maintain the band's direction. "Mike Riley joined the band and he said I basically stepped up I think by default and grabbed the reins and kept trying to steer the buggy"

podcast.title: Resistance to "Country Rock" Label
podcast.body: Pure Prairie League members, including Mike Reilly, resisted the "country rock" label, preferring to call their sound the "midwestern sound" as of June 2021. This preference stems from their diverse musical upbringing in Cincinnati, which encompassed jazz, blues, country, bluegrass, R&B, and soul, leading them to play everything from The Beatles to Lonnie Mack, and being influenced by The Byrds and Poco. "Mike Riley also resist that country rock label even today in June of twenty twenty one he said that the band prefers to think of it as the midwestern sound."
